chapter: Washington clubs, Louis Jordan and Sarah Vaughan, 1949-54
title: The Boston highway crash that left dancer Daisy paralyzed
summary: Sarah rides back with Malachi instead of Joe; moments after Joe speeds past, they find his Cadillac overturned and the chorus girl's spine broken.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: But back to the morning in Boston. We had all gone out there, and we left about 6 o'clock in the morning. Sarah came to me and asked me, "Would you mind if I rode with you'all?
Because Joe has been drinking a little too much. I don't think I want to ride with him." So we said, "Sure!"

In the meanwhile, the theatre that we'd just played in Washington before had a show, and they had a line of chorus girls, who after that engagement were not going to be working for a while. And one of these girls was a friend of Sarah. Sarah asked her to come along with her as an assistant, to help her dress and whatever. Her name was Daisy. I don't remember Daisy's last name. But Daisy was also with Joe. She and Sarah had ridden out there with him.

So when Sarah asked if she could ride back with me -- fine. She gets in the car with us. And we had an expression that we used to use. All bands and groups have things that they say. And when something looks funny or something looks different, we used to just say "There he go" or "There he goes" or something like that. So we were riding down the highway, and we were doing the speed limit, and there's a slight drizzle, rain. All of a sudden, after we had gone about a mile or two, this car whizzed past us, and who was it but Joe Benjamin -- he had Daisy in the car. He honked his horn, and he beeped and passed us and went on. I guess he must have been doing about 60 miles an hour. The speed limit was 40.
Anyway, we just said, "There he go, there he go" and

everybody laughs. About 5 minutes later, the highway looked like it was a little bit more congested than it ordinarily would be. And as we were slowly coming up, we saw Joe's car was turned upside down. He had a Fleetwood Cadillac, four-door. His car was turned upside-down, and he was laying about 20 feet away from it, and the girl was laying somewhere near him, and both of them were moaning in pain. So what was happening, we waited for an ambulance. Of course, the ambulance came and took them to the hospital.

It turned out that Daisy, this dancer, broke her spine, broke it in three places, which meant a never walk again situation. Joe had broken a bone in his cheek, he had a broken bone in his hip and some other lacerations that I don't remember. Anyway, it was a situation where the result was that he was in the hospital for the next I guess three or four months at least. Of course, Daisy, the dancer, was in there for the next two or three years. Finally, she came out and she was a paraplegic for the rest of her life.
